title: Why Anaesthesia Still Lacks an Explanation
topic: the unsettled mechanism of general anaesthesia
paragraphs: Every year tens of millions of people lie down in operating rooms, receive a drug, lose consciousness within seconds, remain still while their bodies are opened, and wake afterward with nothing to report about the interval.
The procedure is also remarkably safe, since death attributable to the anaesthetic itself is now counted in cases per hundreds of thousands.
What is strange about this success is that no one can say, in the way a pharmacologist can say how a blood pressure drug works, what general anaesthesia is at the level of molecules.
The state is defined by what it prevents rather than by what it does.
The first serious answer arrived at the turn of the twentieth century.

Working separately, Hans Horst Meyer and Charles Ernest Overton noticed that if one lines up the anaesthetic agents then available and measures how readily each dissolves in olive oil, that ranking predicts almost exactly how little of each is needed to put an animal under.
The relationship held across more than four orders of magnitude of potency.
A gas that barely dissolves in oil, such as nitrous oxide, has to be given at enormous concentrations.
An agent that dissolves greedily works at a whisper.
The inference seemed forced upon them.
If oil solubility predicts potency, the drug must be working somewhere oily, and the oiliest structure in a neuron is the lipid membrane wrapped around it.
The idea hardened into a single unified account: anaesthetic molecules dissolve into the bilayer, swell or disorder it, and the ion channels embedded there stop working properly.
One observation appeared to seal the case.
Animals anaesthetized and then held under helium at roughly a hundred atmospheres begin to move again, as though the pressure were squeezing the membrane back toward its original volume.
One site, one mechanism, no receptors required.
The account began to fail on its own terms.
The first problem was quantitative.
Warming a membrane by a single degree disorders the bilayer more than a clinical dose of anaesthetic does, yet a mildly feverish patient does not fall asleep.
The second problem was geometric.
Isoflurane exists as two mirror image forms, identical in every property a bath of oil could distinguish, including solubility.
In animals the two differ in potency, one being roughly twice as effective as the other.
Oil cannot tell left from right.
Something with a handed shape, which inside a cell means a protein, must be reading the molecule.
Then came the compounds that refused to cooperate.
Chemists built halogenated molecules whose oil solubility predicted that they ought to be powerful anaesthetics, and several of them are not.
An animal breathing one of these still withdraws from a surgical stimulus at concentrations far above the predicted threshold.
These so called non-immobilizers are not inactive, and several of them impair an animal's memory for what happened while it breathed them.
A compound that erases the record of an event without abolishing the response to it is by itself an argument that the old correlation was never a law of nature.
The gentlest blow was the most damaging.
Firefly luciferase, the enzyme that makes a firefly glow, is a soluble protein floating in water with no membrane anywhere near it.
Anaesthetics switch it off, and they do so in nearly the order of their clinical potency.
If a lone protein in a test tube reproduces the century old correlation, the correlation never pointed at lipid in particular.
It pointed instead at a general fact about these molecules.
They are small, greasy and weakly sticky, and they lodge in any pocket that is oily on the inside, whether in a bilayer or in the folded interior of a protein.
After that, the lipid theory lost its purchase.
The field turned to proteins and found too many of them.

Propofol, etomidate, the barbiturates and the volatile ethers all enhance the GABA type A receptor, the chloride channel that carries most of the brain's inhibition, so that each pulse of inhibition lasts longer than it should.
Glycine receptors, which do similar work in the cord, are enhanced too.
Ketamine, nitrous oxide and xenon leave GABA largely alone and instead block the NMDA glutamate receptor, cutting excitation rather than boosting inhibition.
Volatile agents also open two pore domain potassium channels, which make a neuron harder to fire, and they suppress the pacemaker channels that keep thalamic cells rhythmic.
Mice lacking one of those channels need more agent than their littermates, yet they can still be anaesthetized.
Set the drugs side by side and the problem is visible at a glance.
Xenon is a single atom with a full outer shell that forms almost no chemical bonds, and it is a complete anaesthetic.
Nitrous oxide is three atoms in a line.
Propofol is an oily phenol delivered as a white emulsion.
Etomidate is a small ring compound, alphaxalone is a steroid, and the volatile agents are short carbon chains hung with fluorine and chlorine.
In any other drug class the list would be absurd, since molecules that act at one receptor usually share a recognizable shape.
These share almost nothing beyond a mild reluctance to stay dissolved in water.
Depth, a word used constantly in the operating room, is a metaphor doing a great deal of work.
Its most precise definition is a number called minimum alveolar concentration, or MAC: the concentration of an inhaled agent in the lungs at which half of patients will not move when the skin is cut.
For isoflurane that is a little over one percent, for sevoflurane about two percent, for desflurane about six, and for xenon roughly two thirds of the breath.
For nitrous oxide it is slightly more than a whole atmosphere, which is why that gas cannot carry an anaesthetic by itself.
MAC is both useful and blunt.
It describes a population rather than the patient on the table, and the only thing it measures is whether a body moves.
That last point matters.
Whether a body moves is decided largely below the neck.

In classic animal preparations where the blood supply to the brain and to the rest of the body could be separated, delivering the agent to the brain alone took far more of it to stop movement, and animals whose cords had been cut off from the brain needed about the same concentration as intact ones.
Immobility is mostly a spinal effect.
Unresponsiveness to speech, the thing a patient would call being under, depends on the loops between thalamus and cortex and appears at perhaps a third to a half of MAC.
Amnesia appears earlier still, at something like a quarter of MAC, and leans on the hippocampus and the amygdala.
Three effects, three doses, three places.

General anaesthesia, then, is not one state but a bundle of them, assembled in practice out of several drugs at once: one for unconsciousness, an opioid for the reflex responses to injury, and often a muscle relaxant for stillness.
The relaxant is the awkward member of the set.
It paralyzes the patient and so removes the very sign, movement, on which the standard measure of depth was built.
This is why monitoring depth is harder than it looks.
No instrument reads experience.

The available monitors take the electroencephalogram from a few forehead electrodes, compress it through an algorithm fitted to recordings from patients given particular drugs, and return one number between zero and one hundred.
Those numbers behave well for propofol and the ethers and badly for the rest.
Ketamine, nitrous oxide and xenon can drive the index upward, toward the appearance of wakefulness, in a patient who is entirely unresponsive.
The raw trace is more honest and less convenient.
Propofol produces large slow waves and a band of alpha rhythm that migrates to the front of the head, and at deeper levels the trace breaks into bursts separated by silence.
One old technique makes the difficulty concrete.
Before the muscle relaxant is given, a cuff is inflated on the upper arm so the drug never reaches the hand, and the anaesthetist can then ask the patient to squeeze.
A minority of patients squeeze on command during surgery, and almost none of them remember anything afterward.
Whether such a patient is conscious in any sense that ought to trouble us is not something a monitor can settle, and honest disagreement about it runs through the literature.

Reports of awareness with recall are rare, on the order of one case in twenty thousand when the count relies on patients volunteering the experience, and perhaps twenty or thirty times higher when every patient is asked directly with a structured questionnaire.
The distance between those two figures is itself a finding.
Why has a mechanism been so slow to arrive?
Partly because the targets are redundant.
Delete one of them in a mouse and the anaesthetic usually still works, shifted a little along the dose axis, which is what one expects of a drug that binds many things weakly.
There is a celebrated exception.
Etomidate acts at a pocket in one GABA type A subunit, and changing a single amino acid in that pocket leaves mice the drug can no longer keep still.
That is as clean a result as this field has produced, and it holds for one drug rather than for the state.
A further puzzle is that waking is not induction played backwards, since animals emerge at lower concentrations than were needed to put them under.
None of this unsettles the practice, and it should not.
Anaesthesia is a recipe that works, refined over a century and a half by watching patients rather than by deducing consequences from a theory, and the refinement has been extraordinarily successful.
Medicine has often run this way: lithium and aspirin were in confident use long before anyone could say why they worked.
The incompleteness is a research program rather than a warning.
The situation does have a particular flavor.

The field has learned to produce on demand, and by the millions, a condition it cannot yet define, and the most economical description of what these drugs do is still a list of the things a patient cannot do while they are in the blood.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did Meyer and Overton find when they compared the anaesthetic agents available in their day?
choices: Agents that dissolved most readily in water were the ones that could be given to an animal in the smallest doses
How readily an agent dissolved in olive oil predicted how little of it was needed to anaesthetize an animal
Heavier molecules were consistently more potent than lighter ones
Every agent worked by binding the same receptor in the nerve membrane
The agents varied so widely that no single ordering of them could be found

proof.quote: how readily each dissolves in olive oil, that ranking predicts almost exactly how little

questions.why: Paragraph 2 states it directly: ranking the agents by how readily each dissolves in olive oil predicts almost exactly how little of each is needed. The measurement was solubility in oil, and the finding was a prediction of potency.
distractorNotes: The passage names olive oil, not water, and it later calls these molecules reluctant to stay dissolved in water.
Molecular weight never enters the comparison; the only property measured was solubility.
The lipid account that grew out of the finding was attractive precisely because it needed no receptor at all.
The opposite is stated. The ranking held across more than four orders of magnitude of potency.

questions.stem: The passage reports that anaesthetized animals held under helium at roughly a hundred atmospheres
choices: stopped breathing and had to be supported by a ventilator
needed a far larger dose of agent for the rest of the experiment
showed no measurable change of any kind
began to move again, which was read as pressure restoring the membrane's volume
lost the response to a surgical stimulus that they had still shown a moment earlier

proof.quote: begin to move again, as though the pressure were squeezing the membrane back

questions.why: Paragraph 3 gives this as the observation that seemed to seal the lipid case: under high pressure the animals begin to move again, as though the membrane were being squeezed back toward its original volume.
distractorNotes: Breathing is not what the passage describes. The reported change was the return of movement.
No later dosing is mentioned. The observation was about what the pressure did at the time.
The whole force of the result was that something did change, which is why it looked like proof.
This runs the effect backwards. Pressure brought movement back rather than taking a response away.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 9, which agent has a minimum alveolar concentration greater than a whole atmosphere?
choices: isoflurane
sevoflurane
desflurane
the noble gas xenon
nitrous oxide

proof.quote: For nitrous oxide it is slightly more than a whole atmosphere
for xenon roughly two thirds of the breath

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the MAC of nitrous oxide is slightly more than a whole atmosphere, which is the reason that gas cannot carry an anaesthetic by itself.
distractorNotes: Isoflurane is a little over one percent, the smallest figure in the list.
Sevoflurane is about two percent, far below a full atmosphere.
Desflurane is about six percent, still a small fraction of the breath.
Xenon is roughly two thirds of the breath, high but under one atmosphere.

questions.stem: The passage groups ketamine, nitrous oxide and xenon together because these three
choices: block a glutamate receptor instead of strengthening inhibition
make each pulse of the brain's inhibition last longer than it should
act on the glycine receptors of the spinal cord
open potassium channels that make a neuron harder to fire
are the only agents that can be used without a muscle relaxant

proof.quote: instead block the NMDA glutamate receptor, cutting excitation rather than boosting inhibition

questions.why: Paragraph 7 sets these three apart from the rest: they leave GABA largely alone and block the NMDA glutamate receptor, cutting excitation rather than boosting inhibition.
distractorNotes: That is what the GABA type A group does, and the passage contrasts these three against that group.
Glycine receptors appear in the same paragraph, but they are enhanced by the other group of drugs.
Two pore domain potassium channels are attributed to the volatile agents, not to these three.
The passage never connects any drug to doing without a relaxant.

questions.stem: According to the passage, unresponsiveness to speech appears at roughly what fraction of MAC?
choices: about a quarter
about one tenth
somewhere between a third and a half
the full value of MAC and nothing less
roughly twice the value of MAC

proof.quote: appears at perhaps a third to a half of MAC
Amnesia appears earlier still, at something like a quarter of MAC

questions.why: Paragraph 10 places the three effects on a dose ladder. Unresponsiveness to speech appears at perhaps a third to a half of MAC, above amnesia and below immobility.
distractorNotes: A quarter of MAC is where amnesia appears, one rung lower on the same ladder.
No figure that low is given for any of the three effects.
Full MAC is the immobility figure, the concentration at which half of patients do not move.
Nothing in the passage puts any of the three effects above MAC.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 6, the statement that the lipid theory lost its purchase most nearly means that it lost its
choices: commercial backing from the companies that made the drugs
physical grip on the membranes it described
place in the historical record of the field
power to explain what the evidence showed
supporters among the chemists who first proposed it

proof.quote: the correlation never pointed at lipid in particular
the lipid theory lost its purchase

questions.why: The sentence closes a paragraph about what the old correlation could and could not account for. Purchase here is the hold an idea has on the evidence, so losing it means losing explanatory power.
distractorNotes: Purchase can mean something bought, but no money appears anywhere in this paragraph.
A theory is an idea and not an object, and what slipped was its hold on the evidence.
The passage keeps discussing the theory afterward, so it was not erased from the record.
Who supported the theory is never the subject here. What it could account for is.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 9, "blunt" most nearly means
choices: worn down by repeated use
incapable of fine distinctions
plainly and even harshly worded
slow to take effect in the body
not sharp enough to cut tissue

proof.quote: It describes a population rather than the patient on the table
the only thing it measures is whether a body moves

questions.why: The next sentence in paragraph 9 explains the word: MAC describes a population rather than the patient on the table, and it measures only whether a body moves. That is a measure too coarse to separate cases.
distractorNotes: Nothing suggests the measure has eroded over time. It is coarse from the start.
That is the everyday sense of blunt applied to speech, and here the word is judging a measurement.
Speed of onset is not what the sentence weighs. It weighs how much MAC can tell you.
The literal edge of a blade has no place here, since the word describes a criterion.

questions.stem: The firefly luciferase result best supports which conclusion about the old solubility correlation?
choices: It rested on measurements that later turned out to be mistaken
It applies only to agents that are gases at room temperature
It shows that enzymes rather than ion channels are the real targets
It holds for proteins in a test tube but breaks down in the tissue of a living animal
It fits protein binding just as well, so it cannot single out lipid

proof.quote: the correlation never pointed at lipid in particular
whether in a bilayer or in the folded interior of a protein

questions.why: Paragraph 6 draws exactly this lesson. A protein with no membrane near it reproduces the correlation, so the correlation was never evidence for lipid in particular, only for these molecules lodging in any oily pocket.
distractorNotes: The passage never doubts the measurements. It doubts what they were pointing at.
Nothing restricts the correlation to gases, and propofol is described as an oily liquid.
Luciferase is used as a demonstration, not offered as a target in the brain.
The passage does not set the test tube against the animal here. It uses the test tube to reread the correlation.

questions.stem: Paragraph 11 suggests that a paralyzed patient creates a particular difficulty because
choices: the sign that the standard measure of depth depends on can no longer be seen
muscle relaxants lower the concentration of agent that a patient turns out to need
relaxants are known to erase the memory of the procedure
the opioid in the mixture becomes unnecessary once movement has stopped
paralysis makes the electroencephalogram impossible to record

proof.quote: removes the very sign, movement, on which the standard measure of depth was built

questions.why: Paragraph 11 links two facts: MAC is built on movement, and the relaxant removes movement. With the sign gone, the standard measure has nothing left to read.
distractorNotes: The passage says nothing about relaxants changing how much agent is required.
Amnesia is credited to the anaesthetic at low doses, not to the relaxant.
Each drug in the bundle keeps its own job, and the opioid's job is the reflex response to injury.
The monitors described next read the brain's electrical signal, which paralysis does not silence.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central point of the passage?
choices: The lipid membrane theory has been replaced by a settled account built on one protein target
Anaesthesia carries hidden dangers that patients are never told about, and the profession has been slow to admit it
Anaesthesia works safely at scale yet is not fully understood, with many targets and effects that come apart
The main obstacle to understanding anaesthesia is that operating room monitors are not accurate enough
Because different drugs act at different sites, anaesthetists ought to give only one agent at a time

proof.quote: what general anaesthesia is at the level of molecules
The field turned to proteins and found too many of them.
Three effects, three doses, three places.
a condition it cannot yet define

questions.why: Every section of the passage feeds this claim: the safety record in paragraph 1, the collapse of one theory, the crowd of protein targets, and the separation of immobility, unconsciousness and amnesia, closing with a procedure that works without being defined.
distractorNotes: Half right. The lipid theory did fall, but the passage insists that no single settled target replaced it.
The passage says the opposite about safety and treats the incompleteness as ordinary rather than concealed.
Monitoring is one section of the argument rather than the argument. The trouble starts with the drugs.
The passage treats the multi drug bundle as normal practice and never recommends dropping it.

questions.stem: The author lists xenon, nitrous oxide, propofol, etomidate, alphaxalone and the volatile agents in paragraph 8 mainly to
choices: rank the agents by how safe each one is in practice
show that molecules with nothing structurally in common produce the same state
explain why the volatile agents became the most widely used members of the group
argue that only one drug on the list is a true anaesthetic
demonstrate that every agent named acts at the GABA type A receptor

proof.quote: molecules that act at one receptor usually share a recognizable shape
These share almost nothing beyond a mild reluctance to stay dissolved in water.

questions.why: Paragraph 8 ends by noting that in any other drug class such a list would be absurd, because molecules acting at one receptor usually share a shape. The list exists to make the chemical variety impossible to miss.
distractorNotes: Safety appears in the first and last paragraphs, and no ranking of these drugs is given anywhere.
Popularity is never the subject. The paragraph is about chemical variety.
Xenon is called a complete anaesthetic in this very paragraph, so no member is being disqualified.
Paragraph 7 sorts the drugs by target and places ketamine, nitrous oxide and xenon somewhere else.

questions.stem: Which best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: A puzzle is posed, one explanation rises and collapses, a messier replacement is laid out, and the consequences are weighed
Two rival drugs are compared point by point and one is judged the better choice
A single patient's case is described and then generalized to the whole of surgery
A chronological list of discoveries is given with no argument running through it
A problem in the operating room is described in detail and then a particular piece of monitoring equipment is recommended to solve it

proof.quote: What is strange about this success
One site, one mechanism, no receptors required.
The account began to fail on its own terms.
The field turned to proteins and found too many of them.
not one state but a bundle of them

questions.why: Paragraph 1 poses the puzzle, paragraphs 2 and 3 build the lipid account, paragraphs 4 through 6 dismantle it, paragraphs 7 through 13 lay out the crowded replacement, and paragraphs 14 and 15 weigh what the gap means.
distractorNotes: No two drugs are set against each other as choices. The drugs are grouped by target and by chemistry.
There is no case history anywhere in the passage.
The dates do run forward, but each step is used as evidence in an argument about mechanism.
The monitors are described and criticized, and no particular device is endorsed.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the author's attitude toward the gap between practice and explanation is best described as
choices: alarmed at what the gap means for patients
dismissive of the research that seeks to close it
indifferent to whether patients are safe
untroubled by it and curious about what remains
triumphant about how much has been settled

proof.quote: None of this unsettles the practice, and it should not.
The incompleteness is a research program rather than a warning.
The situation does have a particular flavor.

questions.why: Paragraph 15 opens by saying none of this unsettles the practice and calls the incompleteness a research program rather than a warning, while still pointing out that the field cannot yet define what it produces.
distractorNotes: Alarm is ruled out by the first line of the paragraph, which says the practice is not unsettled.
Calling the gap a research program endorses the work rather than waving it off.
Safety is the first thing the paragraph credits, so indifference does not fit.
The paragraph ends on what the field still cannot define, which is not a victory lap.

questions.stem: The author's handling of the two awareness figures in paragraph 13 is best described as
choices: confident that the lower figure is the accurate one
convinced that the higher figure proves patients are routinely awake and aware during surgery
impatient with colleagues who keep raising the question
certain that the difference is a simple error of record keeping
deliberate about leaving the disagreement open and treating the gap as informative

proof.quote: honest disagreement about it runs through the literature
The distance between those two figures is itself a finding.

questions.why: Paragraph 13 gives both numbers, says honest disagreement about the question runs through the literature, and then calls the distance between the two figures a finding in its own right.
distractorNotes: Both numbers are given without either being endorsed, and the disagreement is called honest.
Almost none of the patients who respond remember anything, and the author declines to say what that amounts to.
No irritation toward anyone appears here. The open question is presented as worth having.
The gap is called a finding, which makes it informative rather than a mistake in the records.

questions.stem: The passage presents all of the following as trouble for the lipid membrane theory EXCEPT
choices: a single degree of warming disorders a bilayer more than a clinical dose does
two mirror image forms of one agent differ in potency
pressure restores movement in an animal that has been anaesthetized
a soluble enzyme with no membrane is switched off in the order of clinical potency
some highly oil soluble compounds fail to keep an animal from moving

proof.quote: Warming a membrane by a single degree disorders the bilayer more than a clinical dose
the two differ in potency, one being roughly twice as effective
they do so in nearly the order of their clinical potency
ought to be powerful anaesthetics, and several of them are not
One observation appeared to seal the case.

questions.why: Pressure reversal is the one item on this list that the passage offers as support for the lipid theory, in paragraph 3, not as evidence against it. The other four all appear in paragraphs 4 through 6 as failures.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 gives this as the first quantitative failure of the theory.
Paragraph 4 gives this as the geometric failure, since oil cannot tell one mirror form from the other.
Paragraph 6 uses luciferase to show that the correlation never pointed at lipid in particular.
Paragraph 5 gives the non-immobilizers, whose oil solubility predicts a potency they do not have.

questions.stem: A reader who wanted to find out which part of the nervous system decides whether a surgical patient moves should turn to
choices: paragraph 3
paragraph 7
paragraph 9
paragraph 10
paragraph 14

proof.quote: Whether a body moves is decided largely below the neck.
Immobility is mostly a spinal effect.

questions.why: Paragraph 10 is where the three effects are assigned to places. It says immobility is mostly a spinal effect and describes the preparations that separated brain from cord.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 covers the lipid theory and the pressure observation.
Paragraph 7 lists molecular targets rather than regions of the nervous system.
Paragraph 9 defines MAC by whether a body moves, but it never says where that decision is made.
Paragraph 14 is about redundant targets and the etomidate exception.
